1072.title: Thirty-nine kinds of work
1072.hook: Shabbat's labors are drawn from building the tabernacle (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)
1072.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat according to halacha study the categories of work and their derivatives, and rabbis apply them to new situations; other Jews keep Shabbat through rest, meals and synagogue in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moed, the order of appointed times, and Rabbi Joshua walking with his staff. Your line: holy time has rules. A new week starts today.

Read the list out loud and something odd happens. Sowing. Plowing. Reaping. Binding sheaves. Threshing. Winnowing. Selecting. Grinding. Sifting. Kneading. Baking. By the end, there's bread on the table. Keep going and a sheep turns into a garment: shearing, washing, combing, dyeing, spinning, weaving, sewing. Then an animal hide becomes a surface you can write two letters on. It's a law, from the Mishnah's tractate on Shabbat. But it reads like a walk through a village from dawn to dusk.
screen: `FIELD TO BREAD.` → `SHEEP TO GARMENT.` → `HIDE TO TWO LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Avot melacha. Avot means fathers, so these are the fathers of work, the main categories. The Mishnah opens its list with the total: forty less one. Back in year one you met the big idea, that the rabbis connect these kinds of work to the building of the tabernacle. Today, the machinery. First, the order. The list follows whole chains of making: bread, then cloth, then the hide for writing, then building and tearing down, putting out and kindling a fire, the final hammer blow that finishes a thing, and carrying from one domain to another. The Talmud asks why baking is on the list when the tabernacle needed dyes cooked, not bread baked, and answers that the Mishnah followed the order of bread. It was built to be remembered, chain by chain. Second, the family. If there are fathers, there are offspring. The rabbis call them toldot: acts that share the father's purpose without looking like it. The Talmud's example: pruning a tree counts under planting, because both help a plant grow. So the thirty-nine aren't a fence around thirty-nine actions. They're thirty-nine questions to ask of any new act: which father does this belong to? Third, why count at all? The Mishnah's own setting is a case of someone who forgot, and in its rulings, how many fathers you broke matters for what you owe. A definition, not a mood. Shabbat doesn't say rest however you like. It says here is what work is, so that what's left over can be rest.

segments.voice: Pick something you did yesterday with your hands or a screen, cooking, typing, fixing, carrying, and play the rabbis' game with it. Is it making something new, changing a thing from one state to another, or moving it from place to place? Find its father, and simply see it as a kind of making; you don't have to stop doing it.
Avot melacha. The fathers of work: the main categories set aside on Shabbat, with their offspring, the toldot, growing out of them. Today's word.
Your line: work, defined. Thirty-nine fathers, and a whole family of offspring. That's today, done.

1073.title: The eruv
1073.hook: a symbolic boundary that turns a neighborhood into one shared home for Shabbat
1073.howItsDone: In some Jewish neighborhoods a community builds an eruv of poles and wire, checks it each week before Shabbat and announces whether it is up; families who rely on it then carry within it on Shabbat. Others who keep the carrying rules carry nothing outside without one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avot melacha, the fathers of work, and your line: work, defined. The last father on the list was carrying from one domain to another. Hold on to that one.

On some street corners, if you look up, you might spot it. Two poles, and a thin wire running across the top, then on down the block. You could walk under it every day and never notice. It holds up no sign and carries no power. But to a family on Shabbat morning, that wire decides whether they can push a stroller to synagogue, carry a house key in a pocket, or bring a dish to a neighbor's lunch.
screen: `TWO POLES AND A WIRE.` → `NO SIGN, NO POWER.` → `A STROLLER ON SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Eruv. Start with yesterday's last father: carrying from one domain to another. Inside your own home you can carry on Shabbat. Out in the public domain, or from a private space into a public one, you can't. The rabbis tie that rule to the Torah's words, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day." So a key, a book, a baby who can't walk yet: all of it stays inside. The rabbis didn't erase that rule. They asked a different question: what is a home? First, a home is shared food. In the Mishnah's tractate Eruvin, the families around a shared courtyard each put in some food, kept together in one house. Now they're one household eating from one table, and the courtyard is theirs. Second, a home has doorways. The Talmud says two posts with a crosspiece over them count as the form of a doorway. Run that doorway around a neighborhood, pole to pole, wire across the top, and the space inside can be treated as one enclosure. Third, a home has to be kept. Communities that rely on an eruv check it before Shabbat, because a broken wire can mean it doesn't hold that week. And not every community uses one. Some Orthodox authorities are strict about which eruvin they rely on, and Jews who don't keep the carrying rules have no need for one. The law about staying in your place is honored, and the neighbors become one place.

Eruv. A shared meal and a boundary of poles and wire that let a whole neighborhood count as one home for carrying on Shabbat. Today's word.

1074.title: Seder and sukkah
1074.hook: tractates on how to hold a seder and how tall a sukkah may be
1074.howItsDone: Jews build a sukkah each autumn, often checking the Mishnah's rules on its height and its roof of branches, and eat in it during the festival; at the Passover seder they drink four cups of wine or grape juice, and communities raise funds so that families who cannot afford a seder can have one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eruv: poles, a wire and a shared meal. Your line: a string makes a home. Today, two festivals and a ruler.

A rabbi stands in a backyard with a measuring stick, squinting up at a hut made of boards and branches. Too tall? Too short? More shade than sun coming through the roof? It looks like a building inspection. It's actually a festival. Inside the order of appointed times sit two tractates that read, at first, like a rulebook for parties. One tells you how to run the Passover seder, cup by cup. The other tells you exactly how tall a sukkah, the harvest hut, may be.
screen: `A RABBI WITH A MEASURING STICK.` → `MORE SHADE THAN SUN?` → `A RULEBOOK FOR PARTIES.`

segments.voice: Seder and sukkah. Start with the hut. The Torah says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days." The Mishnah's tractate Sukkah opens by measuring. A sukkah higher than twenty cubits is not valid, though Rabbi Judah disagrees. Lower than ten handbreadths, not valid. A roof with more sun than shade, not valid. Why so fussy? The Talmud offers a reason for the height: up that high, a person doesn't notice the roof. And the roof is the point. You're meant to sit under it and feel the branches above you, the sky showing through. A sukkah too grand to notice stops doing its job. Now the seder. In tractate Pesachim, the chapter on Passover night opens with the poor. Even the poorest person must not eat that night until reclining at the table like someone free, and must be given no fewer than four cups of wine, even if it comes from the charity fund. Here the measuring sets a floor. Nobody's joy is optional, and nobody's seder is smaller because their wallet is. Put the two together. The Torah also says, "thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." Rejoicing is commanded. And the rabbis treat a commanded joy the way they treat other commands: they ask how, how much, and for whom. A hut you can feel. Cups that reach every table. Joy with a frame around it.

segments.voice: Find something near you, a cup, a table, the width of a window, and measure it slowly, with a ruler or your hands, the way the rabbi squints at the roof. Then ask what it's for: who sits at that table, who drinks from that cup. Let the careful attention turn into a kind of thanks.

Your line: laws of joy. Measured with care, so that joy reaches every table. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1075.title: Esther's scroll and Nineveh's fast
1075.hook: Megillah on reading Esther; Taanit on fasts and rain
1075.carry: read from the page; fast toward a change
1075.howItsDone: On Purim, Jews gather to hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, often making noise at Haman's name; on public fast days, congregations add special prayers and the Torah reading for fasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seder and sukkah: a hut you can feel and four cups for every table. Your line: laws of joy. Today, a scroll and a fast.

Say someone knows the whole book of Esther by heart. Every word, every name, every one of Haman's sons. On Purim night they stand up before the congregation, close their eyes, and recite it flawlessly. A beautiful performance. According to the Mishnah, it doesn't count. The tractate beside it has its own surprise: a public fast where an elder stands up in the town square and tells the crowd that the fasting isn't the point.
screen: `ESTHER, BY HEART.` → `IT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE FASTING ISN'T THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Reading and fasting. First, Megillah, the tractate of the scroll. On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read from a scroll, and the Mishnah sets the terms. Read it out of order, and you haven't fulfilled the duty. Read it from memory, and you haven't either. It has to be read from the written scroll, in order. But for people who speak another language, reading it in that language counts. Strict about the text, generous about the listener. Second, Taanit, the tractate of fasts. Much of it is about rain: when to begin praying for it in the autumn, and what a community does when the rains don't come. The answer is a series of public fasts. On those days, says the Mishnah, the ark is carried out into the town square, ashes are put on it, and the eldest among them stands up to speak. He reminds the crowd of the people of Nineveh, who fasted in the book of Jonah. The verse doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." Works. Not the fast. The fast is the doorway, and the turning is the room. Third, the two belong together, and Esther shows why. Before she goes to the king, she asks the Jews of Shushan to fast for her. The fast comes first, then the brave act. Reading and fasting: both are real only when something actually changes.

Reading and fasting. Megillah, the scroll read from the page in order, and Taanit, the fasts that point beyond themselves to changed works. Today's word.

1076.title: Women
1076.hook: the third order: marriage, divorce and vows
1076.howItsDone: Jewish weddings, divorces and vows follow rules that grow out of this order; Orthodox communities apply them as halacha, Conservative rabbis apply them with their own rulings, and Reform and Reconstructionist couples often adapt the ceremonies so that both partners speak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading and fasting: Esther from the scroll, and a fast that points to changed works. Your line: reading and fasting. Today, the third order.

The third order of the Mishnah has a one-word title: Nashim. Women. Open it expecting a book about women, and you'll find something else. A tractate on what happens when a husband dies childless. One on the marriage contract. One on vows. One on the nazirite, who promises to skip wine and let the hair grow. One on divorce, and one on how a marriage begins. What ties them together isn't a person. It's a promise.
screen: `NASHIM: WOMEN.` → `MARRIAGE, VOWS, DIVORCE.` → `NOT A PERSON. A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Nashim. Here's how the order works. First, it's about bonds you enter by your own words. A marriage begins with an act and words of acceptance. A vow begins when you say it. A divorce ends with a document. Each time, words create something real between two people. The Torah, speaking of vows, says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." That verse could stand over the whole order. Second, why call it Women? Because the world it describes is one where a man usually acted and a woman was acted upon. He gives the ring. He writes the divorce. The Torah's section on vows even goes on to discuss when a father or a husband may cancel a woman's vow; some readers say that's part of why vows sit here at all. It's honest to say it plainly: the Mishnah was written in a world very different from today's, and its frame is a man's. Third, the rabbis also built protections inside that frame, and you'll meet some this week: a contract that guards a wife, a ruling that weeps over divorce, a long struggle for women left stranded. Jews today live with this order in different ways. Orthodox communities keep its law and work within it, for example with prenuptial agreements. Conservative rabbis have added clauses and rulings. Reform and Reconstructionist Jews often reshape the ceremonies so both partners speak and give. What they share is the order's deepest claim: a promise between two people is holy ground. The Talmud even compares a bride to something set apart for the Temple.

1077.title: The marriage contract
1077.hook: an ancient document protecting the wife
1077.howItsDone: At a Jewish wedding the ketubah is signed by witnesses, often read aloud under the chuppah, and given to the bride; couples often frame it and hang it in their home. Orthodox couples use the traditional Aramaic text, while Conservative, Reform and other couples may use adapted or mutual texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nashim, the order of promises people make with words. Your line: covenants between people. Today, one of those promises, on paper.

At a Jewish wedding, under the canopy, there's often a pause. Someone unrolls a document, sometimes painted with flowers and birds and the walls of Jerusalem, and reads it aloud. Guests lean in, expecting poetry. What they hear, if they follow the old text, sounds more like a bank. Sums of money. Property. What the husband owes. What happens to her if the marriage ends. Then the document is handed to the bride, and it's hers. A love story, written as a contract.
screen: `READ ALOUD UNDER THE CANOPY.` → `EXPECTING POETRY.` → `HEARING A CONTRACT.`

segments.voice: Ketubah. Here's what it does. First, it's a promise to her, held by her. The groom takes on obligations in writing, and the wife keeps the document. The rabbis read a verse in Exodus as saying a husband owes his wife food, clothing and her marital rights. The ketubah turns that duty into a signed page a court can enforce. Second, it names a sum. The Mishnah's tractate Ketubot opens with the amounts: two hundred for a woman marrying for the first time, a hundred for a widow. It's money she receives if her husband divorces her or dies. The rabbis argue over these sums for pages, and the arguing is the point: a wife's future was not to be left to her husband's goodwill. Third, it was made harder to escape. The Talmud tells of husbands who, when angry, could say: take your ketubah and go. Then Shimon ben Shetach ruled that all of a husband's property stands behind the ketubah. Walking away was no longer cheap. The contract was a safety net, and a brake. Fourth, it's beautiful anyway. Over the centuries, Jewish communities turned it into art: illuminated pages, gardens and birds around the legal text, hung on the wall of the couple's home. Today couples choose different texts. Orthodox couples keep the traditional Aramaic text. Some Conservative couples add a clause about divorce that you'll hear about soon. Reform and other couples sometimes write mutual promises in both voices. Underneath, the same idea: love is real, and so is the day it might fail, and the vulnerable one should not be left with nothing.

1078.title: Divorce (Gittin 90b)
1078.hook: divorce needs a written document; the Talmud says the altar weeps, yet it is permitted
1078.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Conservative communities a get is written by a scribe and given before a rabbinical court, alongside any civil divorce; Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, and some Reform rabbis offer a ritual of parting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ketubah, the marriage contract the wife keeps. Your line: protection in writing. Today, a harder page.

Some readers say the last page of a tractate is where the rabbis leave something they want remembered. Tractate Gittin, the book of divorce, spends page after page on details: who writes the document, who signs it, how it's delivered. Then, on its final page, the Mishnah records an argument about when a man may divorce his wife, and the Talmud adds one sentence. Divorce is permitted. And yet when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF DETAILS.` → `THE LAST PAGE.` → `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.`

segments.voice: Get. A get is the Jewish document of divorce. First, it has to be written. The Torah describes a man who, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." Not a word spoken in anger, not a door slammed: a written document, carefully made, delivered into her hand. The care slows things down, and it gives her proof that she is free. Second, the argument. The Mishnah records three views about the grounds. The school of Shammai says only for a serious sexual wrong. The school of Hillel says even if she spoiled his cooking. Rabbi Akiva says even if he found someone more beautiful. The rabbis argue, out loud, about how easy it should be to end a marriage, and the law, as later codes follow it, does permit divorce. Third, the tears. Right after this argument, the Talmud quotes a sage: whoever divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears over him. It draws on the prophet Malachi, who rebukes men who cover the altar with weeping, and calls the abandoned wife "the wife of thy covenant." The law stays the law. A marriage that cannot go on may end. But the text refuses to pretend an ending is nothing. Permission and grief, side by side on the same page, like so much of this week: rest given a definition, joy given a frame, a wife given a contract, and now a document that frees, written next to tears.
